conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain for about six days and haven’t been able to keep food down for three days. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been really bad. The pain is constant, and I keep throwing up. I tried to eat a little, but it just comes back up. My stomach feels full all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis, so this could be related to poor blood sugar control or a flare of your chronic condition. Your blood sugar was very high when you arrived—527. We gave you some insulin, and it’s now down to 228.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I couldn’t eat, so I wasn’t sure how much insulin to take. I didn’t want to go too low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’re giving you 80% of your usual long-acting insulin dose since you’re not eating. We’ll keep monitoring your sugars. We also noticed your sodium was low—132—which likely improved with fluids. It’s probably from the vomiting or a condition called SIADH.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had low sodium before. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it drops too fast, but yours was mild and is already improving. You’re drinking now, and your exam shows you’re not dehydrated, so we’re not worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. My pain is still really bad. Can I get something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve given you IV hydromorphone, and you can have it every three hours as needed. We’re also watching for signs of pancreatitis, but your lipase is normal, so it’s likely your usual gastroparesis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why did you use my GJ tube for meds? I didn’t want that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We used it to give you medications since you couldn’t swallow, but I understand you’re upset. We should have discussed it with you first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I pulled it out. I don’t want it anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ve consulted your primary care doctor and psychiatric services. Since you’re not in immediate danger and you’re making this decision voluntarily, we won’t replace it. But you’ll need to care for the site to prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar was 414 this morning, but no ketones in your urine, so it’s not DKA. Your anion gap was slightly elevated but has resolved. We’ll send you home on your usual insulin doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t feel safe going home. My roommate has been sexually assaulting me. I’m scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m so sorry you’re going through that. You mentioned earlier you had thoughts of hurting him. Is that still how you feel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m angry. But I won’t do anything. I just don’t want to go back there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve spoken with a psychiatric nurse who’s supporting you. You’re alert and coherent, and you’re not suicidal. You said you have other places to go—can you stay there safely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I can stay with a friend. I just need my meds and my things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll discharge you home with your usual medications. No changes have been made. You’ll need to keep the GJ tube site clean and dry. Follow up with your primary doctor soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get another GJ tube somewhere else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s something to discuss with another provider. We’re not replacing it here, but you’re free to seek care elsewhere if you choose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? I still need them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll go home with your usual hydromorphone, gabapentin, and other medications. Use them as prescribed. If pain worsens, please reach out to your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my asthma? I haven’t used my inhalers much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lungs sound clear, and your oxygen levels are normal. Keep using your Advair and albuterol as needed. No changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I think I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and please follow up with your primary care provider. If anything changes, don’t hesitate to come back.
